Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

For $m\ge1$, fix a finite family of null hypotheses $H_{0i}$, $1\le i\le m$, before observing the data, and let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be p-value statistics valid for their respective nulls in the sense of [[def-null-valid-p-value-and-fwer-fdr]]. Given $\alpha\in[0,1]$ and an observation $x\in\mathcal X$, order the indices by the pairs $(p_i(x),i)$ in lexicographic order. This gives a unique permutation $\pi$ with $p_{\pi(1)}(x)\le\cdots\le p_{\pi(m)}(x)$; ties are ordered by increasing index.

Set
$$r_\alpha(x)=\max\{k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}:p_{\pi(j)}(x)\le\alpha/(m-j+1)\text{ for every }1\le j\le k\}.$$
The rejected-index set is $R_\alpha(x)=\{\pi(j):1\le j\le r_\alpha(x)\}$. Reject $H_{0i}$ exactly when $i\in R_\alpha(x)$; equivalently, compare sequentially to $\alpha/(m-j+1)$, stop at the first failed comparison, and reject only the preceding ranks.

For $m=0$, extend the procedure to the empty input by returning the empty rejected set. For $m\ge1$, every denominator in a tested rank is positive. The ordering is a unique finite permutation, and the finite set defining $r_\alpha(x)$ contains $0$, so the output is well-defined.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], each $p_i$ is measurable into $[0,1]$ with its Borel trace. For indices $a,b$, the difference $p_a-p_b$ is measurable by [F4], so $\{p_a\le p_b\}$ and $\{p_a<p_b\}$ are measurable preimages by [F5] of the Borel half-lines $(-\infty,0]$ and $(-\infty,0)$. For each permutation $\pi$, its ordering cell $C_\pi$ is the finite intersection over positions $a<b$ of $\{p_{\pi(a)}\le p_{\pi(b)}\}$ if $\pi(a)<\pi(b)$ and $\{p_{\pi(a)}<p_{\pi(b)}\}$ otherwise. These cells are measurable by [F6], and every $x$ belongs to exactly one because lexicographic ordering with index tie-breaking gives a unique permutation by [F3]. For rank $j$, let $Q_{\pi,j}=\{p_{\pi(j)}\le\alpha/(m-j+1)\}$; this pass event and its failure event $Q_{\pi,j}^{c}$ are measurable preimages of Borel half-lines by [F1], [F2], and [F5]. For $k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}$, intersect $C_\pi$ with the pass events for $j\le k$ and, when $k<m$, the failure event at $k+1$. Empty intersections are omitted when $k=0$ or $k=m$. The resulting measurable cell is exactly the event that the order is $\pi$ and the returned prefix length is $k$, by [F3]; these finitely many cells partition $\mathcal X$.

The event $D_i(\alpha)$ is the union of the cells from step 1.1 over all permutations and prefix lengths $k$ with $i\in\{\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(k)\}$. This is a finite union because there are $m!$ permutations and $m+1$ prefix lengths. By [F6], $D_i(\alpha)\in\mathcal A$ for every $i$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), and fix an integer $m\ge1$ before observing the data. Write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. A **finite family of null hypotheses** is a fixed list $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ with each $H_{0i}\subseteq\Theta$. For each $i\in[m]$, let $p_i:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be a p-value statistic ([[def-p-value]]). It is **valid for $H_{0i}$** when

$$P_\theta\{x:p_i(x)\le u\}\le u\qquad(\theta\in H_{0i},\ 0\le u\le1).$$

If $H_{0i}=\varnothing$, this universal condition is vacuous and $i$ never belongs to a true-null index set. For a nonempty null it agrees with the published valid-p-value definition. The family may have any joint dependence among its p-values. Validity is required only under the corresponding null laws; a p-value statistic alone does not imply validity.

For $\theta\in\Theta$, the **true-null index set** is
$$I_0(\theta):=\{i\in[m]:\theta\in H_{0i}\}.$$
A fixed deterministic multiple-testing rule is a family of measurable rejection events $D_i\in\mathcal A$, one for each $i\in[m]$. Its total number of rejections and number of false rejections at parameter $\theta$ are
$$R:=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{D_i},\qquad V_\theta:=\sum_{i\in I_0(\theta)}\mathbf1_{D_i}.$$
Its **familywise error rate (FWER)** at $\theta$ is $P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)$, and its **false discovery rate (FDR)** at $\theta$ is
$$E_\theta\!\left[\frac{V_\theta}{R\vee1}\right],$$
where $R\vee1=\max\{R,1\}$. The random variable $V_\theta/(R\vee1)$ is the **false discovery proportion (FDP)**. Strong FWER control at level $\alpha$ means that this FWER is at most $\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$, including parameters for which only some of the null hypotheses are true. The denominator convention makes the FDP zero when no hypothesis is rejected.

If the testing rule uses auxiliary randomization, include that randomizer in the observation and its sigma-algebra before defining the rejection events $D_i$.

These quantities are well-defined: the finite sums of indicators are measurable, $0\le V_\theta\le R$, and $0\le V_\theta/(R\vee1)\le1$, so the ratio is integrable under each probability law ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).

Let $m\ge1$, let $p_1,\ldots,p_m:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ be p-value statistics on a measurable data space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, and fix $\alpha\in[0,1]$. Define $R_\alpha(x)$ by the lexicographic ordering and passing-prefix formulas of [[alg-holm-step-down-procedure]], applied here to these statistics whether or not they are null-valid. Then each rejection event $D_i(\alpha):=\{x\in\mathcal X:i\in R_\alpha(x)\}$ belongs to $\mathcal A$.

Let $H_{01},\ldots,H_{0m}$ be a fixed finite family with $m\ge1$ in a statistical experiment, and let $p_i$ be a valid p-value for $H_{0i}$ as in [[def-null-valid-p-value-and-fwer-fdr]]. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, reject $H_{0i}$ exactly when $p_i(X)\le\alpha/m$. Then, for every $\theta$ in the parameter space,
$$P_\theta\{\text{at least one true null is rejected}\}=P_\theta(V_\theta\ge1)\le\alpha.$$
The bound holds for every true-null configuration, including the global null and configurations with false nulls, and for arbitrary dependence among the p-values. This is strong FWER control; it is not an FDR guarantee.

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta$ and put $I_0=I_0(\theta)$ and $m_0=|I_0|$. By [F4], the Holm rejection events are measurable, so the FWER from [F2] is defined. If $m_0=0$, no true null can be rejected. Otherwise, let $j_0$ be the least rank occupied by a true null in the ordering from [F3]; it exists because $I_0$ is finite and nonempty. Since [F3] rejects only a prefix, any rejection of a true null forces rank $j_0$ to be rejected. Thus $p_{\pi(j_0)}(X)\le\alpha/(m-j_0+1)$. All $m_0$ true nulls occur at ranks $j_0,\ldots,m$, so $m-j_0+1\ge m_0$ and $\alpha/(m-j_0+1)\le\alpha/m_0$. Hence any false rejection implies $\bigcup_{i\in I_0}\{p_i(X)\le\alpha/m_0\}$.

If $m_0\ge1$, fix $\theta$ and consider the fixed subfamily indexed by $I_0(\theta)$; it has $m_0$ members, all true under this $\theta$, and it is not selected from the observed p-values. By [F1] its p-values are valid. Applying the Bonferroni theorem [F5] to this subfamily at level $\alpha$ bounds the probability of its threshold-union event $\bigcup_{i\in I_0}\{p_i(X)\le\alpha/m_0\}$ by $\alpha$. This contains the Holm false-rejection event from step 1.1, so $\operatorname{FWER}_\theta\le\alpha$. If $m_0=0$, step 1.1 gives FWER zero. Since $\theta$ was arbitrary, the control is strong.

This gives a unique permutation $\pi$ with $p_{\pi(1)}(x)\le\cdots\le p_{\pi(m)}(x)$; ties are ordered by increasing index.

Set
$$r_\alpha(x)=\max\{k\in\{0,\ldots,m\}:p_{\pi(j)}(x)\le\alpha/(m-j+1)\text{ for every }1\le j\le k\}.$$
The rejected-index set is $R_\alpha(x)=\{\pi(j):1\le j\le r_\alpha(x)\}$. Reject $H_{0i}$ exactly when $i\in R_\alpha(x)$; equivalently, compare sequentially to $\alpha/(m-j+1)$, stop at the first failed comparison, and reject only the preceding ranks.

Let $m\ge1$ and let a fixed finite family of null hypotheses and valid p-value statistics be as in [[def-null-valid-p-value-and-fwer-fdr]]. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, let $R_\alpha(X)$ be the rejected-index set from [[alg-holm-step-down-procedure]], and let $I_0(\theta)$ be the true-null index set defined there. By [[lem-holm-rejection-events-are-measurable]], the rejection events are measurable, so the familywise error rate is well-defined as
$$\operatorname{FWER}_\theta=P_\theta(R_\alpha(X)\cap I_0(\theta)\ne\varnothing).$$
Then $\operatorname{FWER}_\theta\le\alpha$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. This is strong familywise error control and requires no independence or other restriction on the joint distribution of the p-values.

derivations.claim: At rank $1$, $1/250<1/80$. At rank $2$, $3/200\le1/60$ because $180\le200$. At rank $3$, $3/100>1/40$ because $120>100$. By [F1] the procedure stops at rank $3$ and rejects exactly indices $\{1,2\}$.

The one-step Bonferroni cutoff is $1/80$. The first p-value is below it; the second is above it because $3/200>1/80$ is equivalent to $240>200$, and the third and fourth are larger still. Thus Bonferroni rejects exactly $\{1\}$, so the two observed rejection sets differ.

This computation determines decisions for one observed vector only. It does not establish that the p-value statistics are valid under their nulls or calculate an error probability; those distributional hypotheses are needed for the guarantee in [F2].
